sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — includes an uncrushed humerus measuring 183 mm in length, offering a rare chance to examine its internal architecture.
This bone featured a thin outer wall filled with spongy tissue made of trabeculae and struts, creating a structure that was both light and strong.
Additionally, the humerus possesses an elongated, unwarped deltopectoral crest, a feature relevant to how the animal moved its wing.
Evidence of guano and fragmented ammonites suggests Bennettazhia ate molluscs and lived in large colonies on cliffs.
In 2025, researchers noted that new remains attributed to Bennettazhia showed no overlap with the original holotype, raising questions about the species' diversity.
Charles Gilmore originally described the remains as a new species of Pteranodon in 1928.
The holotype consists of a humerus, two fused dorsal vertebrae, and a fragment of a joint bone found in the Albian stage of the Hudspeth Formation in Oregon.
Lev Nessov established the genus Bennettazhia in 1991 after reclassifying the remains from a pteranodontid to an azhdarchid.
S. Christopher Bennett later changed his classification in 1994, suggesting the genus belonged to the Dsungaripteridae.
Michael Habib concluded that Bennettazhia belongs to the Azhdarchoidea, a broader group than the Azhdarchidae.
Bennett later established that the genus belonged to the family Dsungaripteridae.
Several authors classified Bennettazhia as a Pterodactyloidea of uncertain affinity (incertae sedis) for many years.
Bennettazhia lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Oregon, United States.
Bennettazhia lived between 113.2 and 100.5 million years ago during the Albian stage.
